summary: Defines how an operator might use part of the MPLS header to encode Explicit Congestion Notification marks. It builds on RFC 3270. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a road gets busy, a signpost warns drivers before cars crash. This puts such warnings into MPLS labels.

questions: how does ecn work in mpls
what is the mpls exp field used for
subtitle: How MPLS routers can use spare EXP codepoints to signal congestion without dropping packets.

tldr.problem: ECN defined congestion marking for IP, but RFC 3270 said nothing about how to carry an ECN mark in the 3-bit MPLS EXP field, which Diffserv already uses.
tldr.mechanism: An operator defines extra EXP codepoints for congestion marked (CM) and not congestion marked (Not-CM), and the egress LSRs check that the transport is ECN-capable before the mark is passed on (per-domain ECT checking).
tldr.outcome: It gives a building block for congestion notification across MPLS domains. It is a Proposed Standard, updates RFC 3032, and is itself updated by RFC 5462.

today: RFC 5129 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3032 and is itself updated by RFC 5462. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Background and Intent
sections.content:
RFC 3168 defines Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) for IP, whose main purpose is to signal congestion without dropping packets. RFC 3270 describes how to support Diffserv in MPLS and allows DSCPs to be encoded in the 3-bit EXP field of the MPLS header, but it says nothing about ECN there.

This document defines how an operator might use some EXP codepoints for ECN, without precluding other uses. Earlier ECN-for-MPLS proposals had fallen by the wayside, and interest returned because ECN for IP became a proposed standard and pre-congestion notification (PCN) was being considered for admission control.

The authors present it as a building block. It does not specify how congestion feedback reaches an upstream node. It does specify how an egress node copies the mark into the IP header if the operator chooses to, but copying is not mandated.
sections.eli5: IP already has a way to say 'this road is getting crowded'. MPLS did not, so this RFC adds one using a tiny field in the MPLS label.

sections.title: Using EXP Codepoints for ECN
sections.content:
The EXP field has only 3 bits, which is 8 codepoints, and Diffserv already uses some. RFC 3270 offers two ways to request Diffserv treatment. With E-LSPs the EXP value indicates the per hop behavior (PHB), so codepoints are scarce. With L-LSPs the label determines scheduling, so there is likely room. The document focuses on E-LSPs as the harder case.

It recommends using codepoints rather than dedicated bits. For each PHB that uses ECN, one codepoint means not congestion marked (Not-CM) and at least one means congestion marked (CM). A PHB with ECN therefore uses at least two EXP codepoints, while a PHB without ECN uses only one.

The remaining problem is making sure an endpoint that does not understand ECN never receives a mark. Three solutions had been proposed, summarized in the table below.
sections.eli5: The label has room for only eight tiny flags. So instead of giving every traffic type its own warning light, a type that wants a warning gets one extra flag value meaning 'crowded'.

sections.title: Per-Domain ECT Checking
sections.content:
The chosen scheme assumes interior LSRs may mark, and checks later. The egress nodes, which pop the last MPLS label (possibly the penultimate hop when penultimate hop popping is used), check whether the packet is headed for an ECN-capable transport. If a congestion marked packet turns out to be Not-ECT, it MUST be dropped there.

Because only egress nodes check, an LSR in the domain MUST NOT be configured to enable ECN marking unless all the egress LSRs around it are already ECN-ready. A domain surrounded by ECN-capable egress LSRs is an ECN-enabled MPLS domain. Some interior LSRs may be legacy. If ECN is not enabled on all egress LSRs, ECN MUST NOT be enabled anywhere in the domain, and congested LSRs MUST drop rather than mark.

The chief drawback is that a marked Not-ECT packet may travel on and be dropped at the egress.
sections.eli5: Routers in the middle may stick a 'crowded' sticker on any packet. At the exit, a guard checks whether the receiver can read stickers. If not, the sticker-bearing packet is thrown away.

sections.title: Push, Mark and Pop Rules
sections.content:
When labels are pushed onto an IP packet, the EXP gets Not-CM if the IP ECN field is Not-ECT, ECT(1) or ECT(0), and CM if it is CE. If several labels are pushed, they all get the same value. When pushing onto an already labeled packet, the topmost EXP value is copied to the new labels.

In an interior node, if the EXP codepoint maps to a PHB that uses ECN and the marking algorithm says to mark, the CM state is set, whether or not it was already set. If the buffer is full, the packet is dropped.

When a label is popped and another remains, an inner Not-CM takes the outer's state; an inner CM stays CM. An inner CM under an outer Not-CM is anomalous and SHOULD be logged.

When the last label is popped, a non-IP payload with no ECT equivalent is treated as Not-ECT, and a CM packet MUST be dropped. For an IP packet, a Not-ECT packet with CM MUST be dropped. If the operator copies the mark into the IP header, the ECN field is set to CE when the EXP is CM, and otherwise left unchanged. At a boundary where a CM packet leaves an ECN-enabled domain for one that is not, the egress checks must be run first.
sections.eli5: Stacking labels is like putting envelopes inside envelopes, and each one copies the warning from the one beside it. When the last envelope comes off, a packet marked 'crowded' that cannot understand warnings is dropped.

sections.title: Deployment Trade-offs
sections.content:
Marking a Not-ECT packet that will later be dropped may waste resources, but only if congestion occurs downstream of an earlier congested queue in the same domain. The authors argue the extra load is bounded by the product of a node's local marking rate and the upstream marking rate, typically two small probabilities multiplied.

They contrast this with the alternative that overloads one bit for ECT and CE. That scheme cannot tell CE from Not-ECT, so a packet already marked and picked again must be dropped. With 6 LSRs in a row, each marking 1% of packets, an already-marked packet is chosen again 0.15% of the time, which the RFC calls an unnecessary drop rate it considers unacceptable for near-zero-loss cores.

Legacy routers in the interior are fine: they simply drop when congested. A legacy router as an egress cannot check ECN capability, so ECN MUST NOT be enabled unless all egress routers are ECN-capable. For L-LSPs, ECN marking SHOULD NOT move packets of one microflow to different LSPs, to avoid misordering.
sections.eli5: The guard sometimes throws away a packet that already travelled far, which wastes a bit of road. The designers decided that small waste is better than a scheme that throws away good packets all the time.

sections.title: Example Uses
sections.content:
The RFC lists several uses. With TCP-style RFC 3168 ECN, an MPLS domain could enable ECN for PHBs such as AF and best effort, so that ECN-capable transports slow down without packet loss. For E-LSPs, an operator with fewer than 8 PHBs could give one PHB a second codepoint for its CM state. As an illustration, the text suggests EXP 010 for not-CM and 011 for CM for the Assured Elastic Treatment Aggregate.

Other uses are congestion-feedback traffic engineering, where an egress LSR tells the ingress about congestion so flows can shift to another path, and PCN flow admission control and termination. PCN needs three states, admission marked, termination marked and not marked, and Appendix A shows how to carry them.
sections.eli5: The warning flag could help normal web traffic slow down, help bosses move traffic to quieter roads, or decide whether new calls are allowed to start.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authors believe no new vulnerabilities are introduced. They considered whether sources could exploit interior LSRs marking Not-ECT packets and relying on the egress to drop them. They conclude sources could already avoid drops by setting ECT.

The ECN nonce from RFC 3540 still works across an MPLS domain without support from this proposal, because the nonce in the IP header is overwritten if an LSR marks congestion. The design does not preclude adding a nonce to the MPLS header later.
sections.eli5: A sneaky sender could not gain much, because it could already dodge the rules in an easier way. The check that catches a cheating receiver still works.
